newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka beefs up air, naval power against Tigers.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka beefs up air, naval power against Tigers.

text.p: Sri Lanka is focusing its military buildup on air and naval forces in a bid to cut off arms supplies to Tamil Tiger guerrillas, military officials said on Monday.
"The most important thing is to dominate the sea, day and night at any cost," said a senior air force official who asked not to be named. "If not, we can't end the war."
Most of the arms used by Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels, fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils, are smuggled in from abroad, he said.
The LTTE, described by defence analysts as a multinational corporation because of its wide overseas network, used to own at least five merchant ships for arms smuggling, military officials said.
The air force and navy have destroyed two such rebel arms ships in the northern waters of the Indian Ocean island in the past two years, one with the help of the Indian navy.

"More emphasis is being given to meeting the threat at sea and to stop LTTE arms smuggling," said a senior navy official. "We want to expand our capability to operate in high seas and intercept and destroy LTTE arms ships. We're an island nation."

Budget estimates for 1997 presented to parliament last week show provisions for acquiring six twin-engined maritime patrol aircraft, the first time the air force is seeking dedicated maritime surveillance capability.

The navy intends to acquire two multipurpose vessels to meet rebel air, surface and underwater threats, nine fast attack craft, two fast gunboats and a fleet of almost two dozen small inshore patrol craft.
The navy is also planning to buy a high-speed hovercraft for amphibious operations and troop transport, officials said.

Deputy Finance Minister Gamini Lakshman Peiris has said 1997 defence spending will be cut to 44 billion rupees (US$786 million) from almost 50 billion rupees this year as the bulk of the arms is being bought this year.
Defence spending was orginally set at 33.9 billion rupees this year but overshot the budget as the government went on an arms-buying spree for intensified operations against the rebels.
"We're spending so much on the war now because we did not spend it (in the past)," the air force official said. "We underestimated the LTTE."
In the past year or so the military has bought Mi-24 helicopter gunships, Mi-17 transport helicopters, An-32 transport planes and big guns from former Soviet Union states.
It has also bought Kfir fighter jets, laser-guided bombs, an unmanned air vehicle for surveillance and Shaldag shallow draught waterjet-propelled fast attack craft from Israel.
China has sold it a corvette-type anti-submarine warfare vessel to counter the threat from rebel underwater suicide squads in the past year, navy officials said.
The military buildup began after the Tigers torpedoed peace talks in April last year by sinking two gunboats in the eastern port of Trincomalee, the navy's biggest base.
A government peace plan offers extensive autonomy to Tamils to try to end the 13-year ethnic war in which the government says more than 50,000 people have died.
Military officials said the LTTE had also acquired anti-aircraft missiles and radars and built up their "Sea Tiger" naval wing recently.
